No MO1550821 update names OneDrive, Entra ID, Azure or Xbox.

sources.fact: Microsoft's final status for EX1550543 (14 Nov 04:15 UTC) and MO1550821 (04:17 UTC) gives this preliminary root cause: a failure in the systems that establish connections to Exchange Online. Traffic shifts during standard network maintenance and upgrades exposed a latent bug, requests queued, and servers ran out of processing capacity. It also says the issue began with an earlier network capacity upgrade and surfaced after a recent network change. There is no authentication, sign-in, routing, identity or Entra wording. Earlier EX1550543 updates: at 01:06 UTC on 13 Nov a process that sets up secure connections was overwhelmed; at 04:59 UTC there was a surge in outbound calls from routing services to backend servers; at 20:01/20:02 UTC sign-in and access could recover before mail delivery caught up. The post-incident report was published in the admin center on 16 Nov at about 04:47 UTC.

disagreements:
1. TM1550488 scope. The brief says TM1550488 covered Teams calendar scheduling and channel creation. Microsoft's own TM1550488 text (Penn mirror) covers chat and messaging in the Americas, 14:45 to 15:53 UTC on 12 Nov, with its own root cause (resource contention) and no link to EX1550543 or MO1550821. Calendar scheduling and private/shared channel failures are in MO1550821's Teams entry (from 00:00 and 02:58 UTC on 13 Nov). On-Site Technology cites TM1550488 and MO1550821 together for those features. Windows Report (blocked for me) reportedly says Microsoft never confirmed a shared cause. The preliminary PIR, as reproduced, puts a Teams gateway failover (01:07 UTC on 12 Nov) in the causal chain, which is not TM1550488.
2. OneDrive. No MO1550821 update ever names it. The preliminary PIR's Service(s) Impacted field names it (Office Watch, 365Fanatic), and news lists include it (Petri, TNW, Windows Central headline). BleepingComputer attributes it to Downdetector only.
3. How many services. Five in Microsoft's first MO1550821 list (18:27 UTC on 12 Nov; BleepingComputer agrees). 19 including Exchange on the public status page per PPC Land, which matches the MO lists from 00:45 to 06:14 UTC on 13 Nov, before Power Apps was added; PPC Land says Power Apps sign-in was not mentioned. 20 in the final MO1550821 list; 22 counting every service ever named. 14 in the preliminary PIR field, which folds the two Defender entries into one, adds OneDrive, and drops the admin centers, Microsoft 365 apps, Education, Graph and Windows 365.
4. Shared authentication and routing layer. Microsoft's November wording is a mid-incident patch to an upstream authentication/routing configuration component that improved stability (admin-center posts, 07:24 to 08:09 UTC on 13 Nov). Microsoft never called it the cause and never called it shared. Its final preliminary root cause (14 Nov) and the preliminary PIR (as reproduced) point to connection-establishment systems, a network gateway and connection negotiation, with no authentication or identity wording. The shared framing comes from Petri's own prose, Science Media Centre experts (Bashroush, McQuiston) and 365Fanatic (a gateway shared with Exchange Online, which is not an authentication layer). The shared identity layer story (Reworked, 16 Sep) and Microsoft's core-authentication-configuration root cause both belong to the 31 Aug to 3 Sep outage (EX1464935/MO1465074).
5. Which way the authentication link runs. PP1550869 and CR1551339 say an authentication dependency service was unavailable, and CR1551339 names Exchange as that dependency. In Microsoft's words, sign-in failed because Exchange failed. Presenc AI's paraphrase is accurate but invites the reverse reading.
6. Sign-in or Entra as a failed service. Microsoft names no Entra or sign-in service failure in any 12 to 13 Nov incident I read. A Hacker News comment relayed by SaaSCity says Entra was fine. A search-engine summary claimed SaaSCity reported Entra sign-in flows down; the page says the opposite. Microsoft did describe sign-in and access improving during recovery (20:01 UTC on 13 Nov; the PIR action log per Office Watch). Sign-in as a symptom is Microsoft-backed; sign-in as a failed service is not.
7. Cause wording drift. At 19:18 UTC on 12 Nov Microsoft said load was not driven by more traffic but by unavailable servers. It later reported a surge in outbound calls from routing services (04:59 UTC on 13 Nov), and the public status page spoke of a traffic influx (flagged by PPC Land).
8. Start time (for the timeline sweep). The mirror's EX1550543 and MO1550821 headers give 10:05 UTC on 12 Nov. The first EX1550543 update is at 16:20 UTC (CIO and Petri put the dashboard start at 16:17 UTC). The PIR gives 16:20 UTC as impact start, TNW gives 16:33 UTC for the first support case, and MO1550821 opened at about 18:26 to 18:27 UTC.
9. Azure. Downdetector and some headlines list Azure. No Microsoft November incident I read names it, Azure status history had no 12 to 13 Nov entry, and ITPro says Azure was not affected.
10. Xbox. Downdetector and the gaming press reported Xbox sign-in and cloud problems on 13 Nov. Kotaku says the Xbox Status page showed everything fine, and Microsoft never tied Xbox to MO1550821.
11. Power Platform. ITPro (unattributed) says the Power Platform Admin Center was unaffected, while Microsoft ran PP1550869 for Power Platform flows, apps and connectors. These are different components, so this is not a real contradiction.
12. Defender for Cloud Apps (08:09 UTC) and Viva Engage (15:52 and 20:01 UTC on 13 Nov) each appear only in interim MO1550821 updates and are missing from the final list.

(B) Only alongside a second independent copy, such as a news outlet quoting the same update. (C) No, Microsoft-hosted pages only, which leaves just Microsoft statements quoted by the press (the five-service first list via BleepingComputer).
chart_feasibility:
Yes, with two caveats. The chart can rest on Microsoft's own words, but those words are Microsoft's Service health text read through a third-party mirror (Penn ISC). And Microsoft describes partial impacts on features that interact with Exchange Online, so the honest label is "listed by Microsoft as impacted", not "down".

Count: 19 services besides Exchange Online in Microsoft's final MO1550821 list (14 Nov, 04:17 UTC): Microsoft 365 admin center, Microsoft 365 apps, Microsoft 365 Apps Admin Center, Microsoft 365 Education, Copilot 365, Defender for Office 365, Defender XDR, Fabric, Graph, Intune, Planner, Power Apps, Purview, Teams, To Do, Power BI, SharePoint Online, Universal Print, Windows 365. If the post means user-facing products only, dropping Graph and the two admin centers leaves 16.

Other counts: 21 if every service Microsoft ever listed counts (adding Defender for Cloud Apps and Viva Engage, each in interim updates only); 13 in the preliminary PIR's Service(s) Impacted field (secondary reproduction, includes OneDrive); 4 in Microsoft's first list (18:27 UTC, 12 Nov).

Leave out TM1550488 (Microsoft never linked it). Leave out OneDrive except via the PIR, and leave out Azure, Xbox and Entra (news or Downdetector only). PP1550869 (Power Platform flows and connectors) and CR1551339 (Dynamics 365 Field Service mobile sign-in) are separate Microsoft advisories and can go in a footnote.

The most faithful chart is a step chart of Microsoft's own list, each step stamped with a Microsoft update time (services besides mail): 4 at 18:27 UTC on 12 Nov; 7 at 19:58; 10 at 20:57; 12 at 22:03; 13 at 22:58; 17 at 00:00 UTC on 13 Nov; 18 at 00:45; 19 at 06:54; 20 at 08:09; back to 19; 20 at 15:52 and 20:01; 19 from 22:00 through the final update. Re-count from a raw capture with a script before publishing.

Question for the owner (multiple choice). Q1: which count should the chart show? (A) 19, Microsoft's final MO1550821 list besides Exchange Online (recommended). (B) 21, every service Microsoft listed at any point. (C) 13, the preliminary PIR field (includes OneDrive; secondary reproduction only). (D) The timestamped step chart, from 4 up to the final 19.
